title: Wilderness Dharma Practice
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of connecting with nature as a means of deepening one's spiritual practice in Zen. By spending time in solitude or community in natural environments, individuals can simplify their lives, cultivate a sense of connection with their true nature, and discover a deeper reality that transcends the fleeting moments of life. This approach to wilderness Dharma practice aims to create a sense of renewal, community, and connection with the natural world, allowing participants to explore their spiritual lives in a way that is both personal and communal.

sentences.text: Good evening.

I'm going to talk tonight about wilderness dharma practice that our sangha has been engaged with for the last ten years or so, and how we came to start doing that, where it fits in what's going on with Zen practice in North America, and where it might go.
For me personally, it sprang out of the way I got involved in Zen.
When I started practicing zazen years ago, I didn't really get into it on a formal level at the beginning.
I didn't join a group or even have a group anywhere to join for a number of years, maybe eight years or so.
So I would sit on my own, and it was not something that happened on an everyday basis.
But it would happen more when I really had the time.
When it really seemed to fit was especially when I would go out in the back country on backpacks.
Then it seemed as though life got reduced to a certain basic set of moves, and zazen fit as being part of that scene, that scenario.
So right from the beginning, it seemed to me that zazen practice and leaving the city, going into nature, were things that fit together.
Later, when I started formal Zen practice and was going to retreats in zazen, this sense of correspondence between an experience like zazen and a back country experience just seemed to be reinforced.
There was something similar.
You reduced or simplified your life.
You took ultimate responsibility for every little thing that made your day work.
Your needs and wants, and the things that were supplying them, were reduced to a very basic set of circumstances and items.
And that seemed to correspond.
One thing that didn't correspond was my companions.
I always felt an incongruency in going out in the back country with people who might be friends or whatnot, but it would be a sort of chatty experience.
I often felt this experience needs a better social container, because it's too special to be talking about the latest TV show or the football game or whatever was the current topic of chatter.
So I always felt as though I wanted to bring those two experiences into closer contact, into some kind of better container.
It really wasn't until beginning to do these retreats with our group that I was able to say, okay, this is how we can do it.

It was the introduction of the formal aspects of our Zen practice into the back country experience that gave it the shape that allowed everyone participating to go into the experience with a similar set of expectations about how to proceed together.
I've been asked a few times over the years, why the wilderness?
Doesn't that seem sort of extreme?
Or isn't it analogous to the loosey-goosey educational fantasies from the seventies of backpacking for credits?
It's not real spiritual experience, it's not real education or whatever.
You're combining your recreation and your spiritual life, aren't you?
Why the wilderness?
Well, a few things about it.
In my mind I see it as being beyond the human realm and getting in contact with the human-nature intersection.
To me that seems crucial to the basic spiritual question for humans.
We seem to be some different kind of animal.
Although we are animals, we have this curious intellect and we conceptualize and remember.
In a sense we have this trouble with fitting in with nature.
That seems to be a crux of what's going on with us as spiritual beings: getting right with what's going on with the place we live.
I've always been intrigued by that phrase, true nature, when it's applied to us.
What is our true nature?
Also, the wilderness container created that place for group cohesion.
The group going into the wilderness suddenly becomes a group in a very palpable, felt sense.
That seemed to be a really useful way to bring a group together that is questing and exploring.

Another thing about going to nature is the sense that perhaps somewhere out there, who knows, are actual places, power places, important centers, things maybe that we don't understand or haven't identified.
But if we go, maybe we'll see, maybe we'll feel that a place is special in a way that we have difficulty sometimes feeling when we're surrounded by our own built environment.

And there's also the process of going into the wilderness, the process of coming back, this going and returning process that, for instance, Norman in his book *Sailing Home* speaks about as being fundamental to our spiritual life, that our life is a life of returning.
Just as on the cushion we return to the breath over and over again.
In our tradition we can look at Shakyamuni as being an archetype of going to the wilderness, because this is what he did.
He left the palace, he left the civilized built environment and he went off to the woods, he went to the mountains, and that's where he experienced his realization.
He did that not out of some novelty but because that was really an established pathway in his culture, for seeking.
Sages lived off in the mountains and they lived in the caves.
Something like that is not just from that culture but has been a pattern across all human cultures.

We can look at Native Americans on this continent, but really it applies to all pre-civilization people: that was a predominant mode, to go to the wilderness to seek inspiration or insight, enlightenment, messages.
Even nowadays there are elements of our tradition that still practice somewhat in these ways.
In fact, right now Tim is in Japan, and one of the places they're going to be visiting is Mount Hiei, where the Marathon monks live.
We have a nice book in our library about them, and apparently a monk, Endo Mitsunaga, recently completed the cycle of practice for monks at Mount Hiei.
He's only the thirteenth one to complete the cycle since the World War II era.
If you read the book you'll understand why this is difficult.

It's a multi-year process, each year progressively harder, where essentially every night you run slowly about a marathon's distance around Mount Hiei, stopping at spiritual shrines along the way, getting a few hours' sleep a night, and then doing all your [unclear: "templatures"] during the day, and then doing it again the next night.
They do that for like a hundred days in a row or something like that, and then they do it again.
They do it while wearing these woven grass sandals and their monk robes.
It's really over the top.
In America we have that same tradition that we can point towards, of retreating to the wilderness for inspiration.
There's the lesson of Henry David Thoreau.
When I was a young person, before I got into Zen and Buddhism, I was very inspired by reading *Walden*.

I was drawn to that book when I found out the basic storyline of it, and I thought, oh okay, because this just seemed like the quintessential American archetype of someone going to the woods and finding out what that meant, what it meant to be alone, what it meant to be with nature, and how to relate to people within that context.

Here in the Pacific Northwest, years ago, Gary Snyder and some of the other beat poets spent seasons up the Skagit as fire lookouts and went there specifically to have a similar Thoreauvian kind of existence, a place far away where they had their little hut on top of mountains, like Chinese hermits really, who were named for mountains, like the Chinese poet Han Shan.
Shan means mountain, so there is a mountain named Han Shan and there's a poet named Han Shan who's from the mountain Han Shan.
This was typical: abbots of temples would sometimes be named for the mountain that the temple was on.

The way this wilderness Dharma hiking practice evolved in North America, it really started with Gary Snyder down in the Bay Area, initially with Allen Ginsberg and a few others, doing a ritual circumambulation of Mount Tamalpais.

To this day, maybe forty or more years later, people still do that circumambulation annually, and because of that intent and practice, the mountain is now pretty widely regarded in the Bay Area as being a special place.
The intention has been put there.

After forming Ring of Bone Zendo in the foothills of the Sierras, Snyder started a hiking practice where they would do sesshin as a backpack, and Ring of Bone Zendo still does this practice twice a year, seven-day-long sesshins as backpacks.
So currently the extent of wilderness Dharma practice that's happening in North America is pretty limited.
There's Ring of Bone Zendo.
As I search the internet, I see Treetop Zen Center in Maine, which is with the White Plum Asanga lineage, doing significant backcountry retreats.

Outside of those two, I have seen Upaya Zen Center in New Mexico doing retreats, but most of those seem to be led by leaders on contract as workshop-type events, not so much created within the Sangha.
Others will do retreats that are lodge-based, where every day you might hike but you're back at a lodge, so not really backcountry-type retreats.
And then there's us, and we've been doing that for ten years.
In a sense we're working on something that not many people are working on, and it's pretty interesting.
Each group that does this, since it's a pretty new, limited, self-created kind of thing, has a different way of doing it.
The Ring of Bone Sangha seems to take the form of mostly going to a different place each time.
They don't go to the same place; they explore new territory.
In that sense they seem to take on the mind of the recreational hiker who wants to explore new territory.
In the spring they usually head far afield to the south, maybe to the southwest, someplace warm, and in the summer they stick closer to home.
Being in the locale they're in, they have the ability to move around, not too far north or south, and hit good weather almost any time of the year, east or west of the mountains.
So they have that advantage.
In that sense they've adopted a practice that moves around in that environment and takes advantage of it.
It sounds like their retreats respond to the place that they're going to.
Sometimes they'll change camp every night, hiking down the trail, or maybe they'll stay a couple of nights in one place and then move.
A recreational backpacker would ideally like to do a loop trip, wouldn't that be nice, rather than repeat territory, so maybe they try and do that, or they go out and back.
But to look at the wilderness Dharma practice, what sort of form can that practice take?
You take the basic ingredients of Zen practice: zazen, kinhin, zazen, kinhin, dokusan, teisho, lecture.
You combine that with this action of picking up your little turtle of a home on your back and walking.
What sort of form can that take?
One could be a recurring pilgrimage, in other words going to the same place every time, which would reinforce a sense of place.
It could be circumambulating a spot, which is similar to what was done in ancient times at Buddhist stupas, a ritual of circumambulation around a ritual spot.
It could take a form of what I call a walkabout practice, similar to Australian aborigines, where you just go off, you cover the territory, and you discover what you find.

It could be a vigil practice, where you stay in one spot for a specific duration to sit out and witness, or keep vigil for an event, a sunrise, throughout a night, to witness an event like an eclipse, or to wait upon the return of someone who has gone out, being basically watchful for them.
It could be an open, borderless, timeless sort of practice.
In other words, you go to a spot and you mark out a ritual spot that you don't leave, but it represents the universe, and that would be a place where you would then stay for as long as it takes.
That would be like a Shakyamuni-type practice.

It can be having nature as a focus for your practice through the senses: listening practice, gazing practice, gazing into the sky practice, opening yourself to different sensory awarenesses, for which nature provides a rich field.

And it can be an exploration of liturgy too, sutras, and also maybe unconventional liturgy that speaks of nature, that you then map onto the experience of traveling in nature, so that the liturgy and the travel become one.
In other words, sutras for walking.
The way we do our wilderness retreats combines a number of these elements.

We begin our retreats with an idea of a community blessing, in that we gather together outside in a cedar grove with members of the community who are there to witness the departure of the retreatants, the smaller group heading to the wilderness, and to wish them well.
We go through a ritual of renewal and purification with a sweat lodge ceremony.
This forms a portal through which we can set and speak intentions about the type of energy we want to bring consciously to what we're about to step into.
We follow a set route that we've followed now for ten years.

We drive up the Skagit Highway 20 and up the west side of Baker Lake, and we get to Road 12 and we turn and follow Road 12 to its end, which is the back side of the Twin Sisters, between there and Mount Baker.
We've been very fortunate to discover this trail, because it seems to be almost never used, and yet it accesses an area that a lot of people would like to hike.
However, they all seem to come up this other trail, up Road 13, which is a much more difficult trail but it's shorter, and it goes straight to these high alpine meadows.

It's just the kind of thing that people going out for a day hike will want to get to whereas the trail we hike on meanders up more gradually through heavy old growth hemlock forest, crossing some streams, going over a low pass and sneaking up into a little subalpine meadow.

The other hikers coming from the other direction can get there, but they would have to drop down 400 feet of switchbacks and then turn around and go back, and most of them don't want to do that, so they don't come down.
We stop along the way, hiking silently, and we have special stops that we've always stopped at along the trail where we perform rituals and chant sections of the mountains and river sutra.
By the end of the weekend, having traveled up and then back, we've made five different ritual stops and we have worked our way through the sutra, so we do sutra walking in that sense.
While we're up at our base camp we have a log shelter that's available.
It's actually not technically wilderness area designation where we're at, but national recreation area, so they allow this building to remain.
If it was a wilderness area they'd let it deteriorate and go away.
But there's a nice little shelter and we can set it up as a little zendo and do a regular schedule.

We respond to how back country retreat needs to function by having periods of the day that are totally silent and periods of the day where we break silence and deal with camp chores and just what needs to be done.

Then in the mid morning in the middle of the retreat we have a period of time when the retreatants get set out in different special spots of their own for a solo, a time when they're just alone in a small area.
The way we do that is as though it were dokusan.
In other words, we are sitting in our zendo and from that each person is taken out to their spot and left there, and when they're brought back we're sitting in zazen again.
So it's similar to how it would be in a retreat if you were asked to come to dokusan.
Another part of what we do is we've written a dedication, or we adapted a dedication that I found from Zen Center Rochester.
All of our rituals and services we finish up with this special dedication that we've developed for these nature-based retreats, and it goes like this:
*We've offered candles and incense and chanted the mountains and river sutra.
Whatever merit comes to us from these offerings we now return to the earth, sea and sky.

Let us now each in turn dedicate our gratitude to nature, remembering the stillness, the clarity, the kindness that is the real nature of all life; remembering the way of life day by day that accords with Buddha; and remembering the community of all beings that is our inspiration and support.
May the air be left pure, may the waters be clean, may the earth be restored, may we attain Buddha's way together with all beings.*
Then we finish it in our normal fashion.
If you were listening carefully you would sort of see that basically that's a dedication to the three treasures, but reworded in a nature-based sense.
When we're hiking and doing this retreat we bring our roles that we usually have in a Zen retreat along with us.
We have a tanken, a timekeeper, who serves a very important function during the retreat.
During the hiking portions of the retreat the tanken will be at the front of the line, and we need to take regular rest intervals to keep everyone together and well rested.

The tanken is responsible for judging the terrain, shortening the hiking periods when the terrain is more difficult, lengthening them slightly when the terrain is easier, and stopping us for rest intervals so we can gather together.
We hike with a system that allows us to hike and stay safe and together but stay silent.

The system hinges around a couple of simple rules, the most basic of which is that it's incumbent upon each person to be responsible to maintain a verbal communication distance with whoever is behind them.
Then we have the tanken at the front of the line and we'll usually have a sweep person at the end of the line, so nobody should go ahead of the tanken and nobody should go behind the sweep.
This allows the line to stay together, to stay in communication even though we don't need to talk.
We have a tenzo cooking, and eating is really important in the back country.

Someone is involved with the food before the trip even starts: organizing it, getting it together, weighing it so that everyone is carrying bags of equal weight of group food, and then heading up the cooking chores in camp.
And we have doshis to help us lead the rituals.
We bring our rakasus, we bring our okesas, and we put them on at the trailside and do full prostrations on the dirt and to trees and to waterfalls and to valleys and to mountains.
We have a special way of wrapping ourselves in our sleeping bags, called a sleeping bag okesa, because sitting meditation outdoors can get cold, even if it doesn't seem like it's cold.
Once you're sitting still for a little period of time, that thin breeze gets really cold, especially at six or seven or eight in the morning.
We can't bring zabutons and zafus with us in our backpacks, so we take our sleeping pads and roll them up but leave a little bit sticking out for our legs to lay on.
Then we can sit on the roll of our sleeping pads, and we can fit our sleeping bags here and wrap them around us in a particular way that leaves us just cocooned up, just like an okesa.
And we chant the mountains and river sutra, which is a very inspiring, confounding, interesting text.
It's always surprising, even after years of working with it.
There's always something that you didn't remember from before that comes up.
Chanting a sutra in a ritual manner like this over a number of days is a very, very, very interesting way to experience a sutra, outside of just the normal process of reading it.
There are many writings that could be conducive to use in this type of wilderness dharma practice.
We've done hikes in the Chuckanuts where we chanted the Genjokoan.
I've given lectures before the retreat based off of Henry David Thoreau's essay "Walking," in which he begins the essay by saying:

*I wish to speak a word for nature, for absolute freedom and wildness, as opposed to a freedom and culture merely civil; to regard man as an inhabitant, and a part and parcel of nature, rather than a member of society.

I wish to make an extreme statement, if so I may make an emphatic one, for there are enough champions of civilization: the minister and the school committee and every one of you will take care of that.*
It's a sort of statement of defiance about claiming original nature.

So the future of this kind of practice seems to be going strongly with us, and it seems to me that many sanghas in this country could hopefully benefit from finding a way to integrate this type of practice, because our spiritual practice and the place we live in need to come together.
We need to establish sacred sites, sacred pathways, pilgrimages, circumambulations.
In other parts of the world billions of people still follow pilgrimages, but in our part of the world it seems as though nothing's really sacred, and that seems to be a real problem for us.
If places and pathways were sacred, then our relationship to ourselves, to each other and to the place we live would be fundamentally different.

We can create accessible means, small ways to step out in nature: hills and streams, retreats, places where those who can't put on a backpack and hike all the way up the trail can still participate with the same sort of elements that this sort of practice provides.
Doing this sort of practice instills an important sense of stewardship.
Stewardship is a spiritual practice, taking care of the place we live in.
We can also not imagine the wilderness as being separate from our daily lives.

We can acknowledge the greatness of nature right here: the sun, the moon, the stars, their changes, their cycles, the tides, the seasons, the migrations, birds and salmon, the leaving, the leaving, the returning.
That is really the root and the heart of what our practice feels like.
So to sort of cap this off, I thought that I would suggest a little addition to our schedule coming up.
I saw Saturday, August 7th was the first Saturday where we're doing some practice here in the hall, and I thought, what a great day.
Maybe some folks after morning practice would like to get in some cars and head to one of our most important sacred sites in this county, that is sort of hidden.
Some people know about it and some people don't, but it's just not celebrated enough.
That's the old growth at mile post 43 on the Mount Baker Highway.

Years ago, when the national forest system was established, somebody with a little bit of foresight thought, maybe we should set a few little pieces of it aside, and so they made these natural history research areas scattered here and there about the national forest system of the west.
One of them is right alongside the highway near mile post 43, and it's never been cut, and the forest service wisely doesn't mark it.
They'll tell you where it is if you ask.
There's a little pullout where maybe two or three cars can pull out, and a path heading in, and you can walk in a few hundred feet, a couple hundred yards.
I don't think the trail goes more than a quarter mile.
But the trees are about as big in diameter as this circle, they're huge, and you can look up 200 feet and you don't see a branch.
It's a pretty special place.
So I thought maybe we'd go up there and maybe chant some sutras and spend a little bit of time and then come on back.
I'll be planning on doing that and other people are invited, August 7th.
I thought I'd finish up.
Some people know that just last week I made an attempt on climbing Mount Baker with my son.
It was a big trip, and we had some friends from out of town.
We went up the eastern glacier, which is that same side of the mountain where we've been going with the Zen retreats.
We were just basically just above the little hut down there, we could see where that was, right down there in that meadow.
We came up the road 13, we did the tough stream crossing and came up to the high camp, and in the early, early morning, three in the morning, we set out for the summit.
I decided to recite this poem that I wrote years ago after I climbed Mount Hood.

We saw this phenomenon years ago on Mount Hood where, when the atmosphere is just right, there is a moment, and it's really only a short moment, when the light's barely beginning to come up and the mountain projects an immense shadow out over the landscape, a distinct immense shadow.
Then a moment later the light's too great and the shadow disappears.
I called the poem "Because It's Always There," which is sort of a play on that old thing, like, why did you climb the mountain?
Because it's there.
I don't know who said that, but this is sort of a little twist on that idea.
*The moment of light coming up projects the mountain onto a million acres, its fragile shadow is a long gray point.
From here the curve of the planet is easily seen, making an arc around my two feet in the snow.
I must use now as little as I possibly can of the things I usually need.
The trees below are spaced like footprints across the edges of boulders the glacier has carefully gathered.
These last trees are twisted from the pressure of thin air and thick snow.
They use less air, less soil, less of themselves, in more light, more water, but none to drink.
This place reflects more, less or more, of all the amounts we need.
This then is a kind of desert.
These trees are like the frontiers of trees, and here the upper slopes seem to be always erupting out of the forest into a pyramid that never changes.
And the only smell is my own sweat and many square miles of frozen water. [unclear: "any hints"] come up over the snow so lightly, almost without wind, only tapping the shoulder, memory.
From here into the horizon, white, green and blue, the world is simple where the life gives out.*
And I think that's why we go to the wilderness.
We go to the wilderness to understand something about life and death, something about our true nature, the nature of the world we live in, something about a place beyond life and death.
